item.title: High Court to rule tomorrow on Ketan Lal’s application for interim orders to halt the progress of the Constitution Bill
item.description: High Court Judge, Justice Dane Tuiqereqere will deliver his judgement at 2.15pm today on independent MP Ketan Lal’s application for interim orders to halt the progress of the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026. Lal's application seeks orders restraining the Speaker of Parliament from notifying the President if the Constitution Amendment Bill is passed with the two thirds support required for conduct
item.content:encoded:
High Court Judge, Justice Dane Tuiqereqere will deliver his judgement at 2.15pm today on independent MP Ketan Lal’s application for interim orders to halt the progress of the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026.

Lal's application seeks orders restraining the Speaker of Parliament from notifying the President if the Constitution Amendment Bill is passed with the two thirds support required for conducting a referendum.

Lal's lawyer Mohammed Saneem argued whether the voting threshold used in Parliament for a Constitutional Amendment Bill complied with the constitutional requirements.

He also questioned whether the required two-thirds majority should be calculated based on Parliament's full membership or the number of members present.

The Speaker's legal counsel, Seforan Fatiaki says the parliamentary process is not completed as yet.

He says the process ends with the notification by the Speaker to the President after the third reading if the Bill gets the support of two thirds of parliament.

Fatiaki says this constitution amendment process started in parliament in 2025 and then they went to the Supreme Court, and the court then gave it's advice.

He adds since two parliamentary seats are vacant, the threshold should be two thirds of the 53 Members of Parliament in the third reading of the Constitution Amendment Bill in parliament.

item.title: Rarawai Mill to close next Wednesday as growers urged to complete harvesting
item.description: Cane growers and harvesting gangs supplying the Rarawai Mill are being urged to harvest and deliver all remaining cane next Tuesday, ahead of the mill's scheduled closure for the 2026 crushing season on Wednesday. The Sugar Cane Growers Council is calling on all growers to speed up harvesting and deliveries to ensure as much cane as possible is processed before the crushing season ends.
item.content:encoded:
Cane growers and harvesting gangs supplying the Rarawai Mill are being urged to harvest and deliver all remaining cane next Tuesday, ahead of the mill's scheduled closure for the 2026 crushing season on Wednesday.

The Sugar Cane Growers Council is calling on all growers to speed up harvesting and deliveries to ensure as much cane as possible is processed before the crushing season ends.

Meanwhile, the Lautoka Mill is scheduled to close this Sunday, with growers urged to harvest and deliver all remaining cane by Saturday.

The Labasa Mill is expected to close on 6th November, and growers and harvesting gangs in the area are being urged to complete all harvesting and deliveries by 5th November.

item.title: FWCC calls for withdrawal of draft Constitution
item.description: The Fiji Women’s Crisis Centre is calling on the Fiji Government to withdraw the current draft Constitution, take seriously the feedback already given by the people, and return with a proposal that genuinely reflects Fiji’s evolving democracy and the aspirations of Fijians in all their diversity. FWCC Coordinator Shamima Ali says you cannot claim to be strengthening democracy while losing sight of
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Women’s Crisis Centre is calling on the Fiji Government to withdraw the current draft Constitution, take seriously the feedback already given by the people, and return with a proposal that genuinely reflects Fiji’s evolving democracy and the aspirations of Fijians in all their diversity.

FWCC Coordinator Shamima Ali says you cannot claim to be strengthening democracy while losing sight of the very people democracy is meant to serve.

She says people are struggling with the rising cost of living, poverty remains a serious concern for families and communities, health infrastructure and services are under pressure, while many communities continue to face unreliable access to basic services, including water and cimate pressures, including El-Nino conditions, are adding to the challenges people already face.

She says these are the everyday realities of people trying to provide for their families, access essential services and cope with increasing financial pressures.

The Coordinator says the constitutional change is consuming the national conversation while urgent economic, social and environmental pressures continue to affect families and communities.

She says this almost seems, deliberate to distract people from the real issues.

FWCC is calling for a constitutional process that listens meaningfully to the people, respects the diversity of views across Fiji, and strengthens public confidence in the country’s democratic institutions.

They add that any Constitution must embrace the universal human rights of all people.
